title: Certainty of intention and subject matter
subtitle: Reading trust language closely — and the tangible/intangible split the courts haven't fully resolved
objectives: State Knight v Knight's three certainties and explain why a trust fails without each of the first two
Distinguish precatory language from an imperative intention to create a trust, and apply that distinction to unfamiliar wording
Apply the two limbs of certainty of subject matter — certainty of the trust property, and certainty of the beneficial shares — to new fact patterns
Explain the tangible/intangible property split between Re Goldcorp Exchange and Hunter v Moss, and state honestly why that split remains doctrinally contested

leadingAuthorities.role: States the three certainties a valid express trust requires
Certainty of intention can be found in a course of conduct and repeated informal statements, without technical language
Intention to create a trust inferred from segregating funds, without the word 'trust' ever being used
'The bulk of my estate' held too uncertain to identify trust property
No trust over unascertained tangible goods (bullion) not segregated from a general stock
Controversially allows a trust over an unsegregated part of an intangible, fungible holding (shares)

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson rewards slow reading and punishes skimming. Most of the marks lost on certainties questions come from students who correctly recite the three certainties, then misread the actual wording of a will or declaration under exam pressure. The skill this lesson builds is close reading, not memorisation.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You already know the rules here. The test pool is weighted toward application — expect wording you have to parse carefully, not definitions to recall.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Anchor yourself on Knight v Knight in Part 1 before anything else. Every later part in this lesson assumes you can state the two certainties covered here without hesitation.

overview.hook: A grandmother writes in her will that she leaves 'the bulk of my estate' to her granddaughter, 'in full confidence that she will do right by her sisters'. A businessman tells his partner, over and over, 'this money is as much yours as mine.' A company facing bankruptcy opens a separate bank account for customer prepayments and calls it nothing in particular. Only one of these three creates a trust with total certainty — and the other two sit right on the line courts have spent 150 years arguing about. This lesson is about reading the words that decide which side of that line you're on.

parts.heading: Knight v Knight and the checklist equity insists on
parts.voice: forensic — sets up the doctrine as a precise test to be applied, not a general idea
body: Lord Langdale MR, in Knight v Knight (1840), distilled what any express trust requires down to three certainties: certainty of intention (did the settlor actually intend to impose a binding trust obligation, rather than expressing a hope or a wish?), certainty of subject matter (is it clear exactly what property is held on trust, and in what shares the beneficiaries take it?), and certainty of objects (is it clear who the beneficiaries are?).

This lesson covers the first two in depth. Miss any one of the three certainties, and the trust fails — not partially, not 'probably', but completely, as a matter of law. That has real consequences: property that was meant to pass on trust instead usually results back to the settlor's estate, defeating exactly the intention the document was trying to express.

Treat the three certainties the way a examiner treats them: as a checklist to run through methodically on every trust problem, in order, before you say anything else about the facts. Skipping straight to 'is this a valid trust?' without checking each certainty in turn is the single most common way students lose easy marks on this topic.

components.label: Knight v Knight: the three certainties
points: Certainty of intention — the settlor must have intended to impose a binding trust obligation, not merely to express a hope, wish or moral expectation
Certainty of subject matter — the trust property must be identifiable, and (where there is more than one beneficiary) the beneficial shares must be identifiable too
Certainty of objects — the beneficiaries must be identifiable with sufficient certainty (covered in a later lesson on certainty of objects and discretionary trusts)

interaction.prompt: Name the three certainties required for a valid express trust, as stated in Knight v Knight.
acceptableAnswers: certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter, certainty of objects
interaction.modelAnswer: Certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter, and certainty of objects — all three must be present, or the trust fails.

parts.heading: Precatory words: when 'I wish' isn't a trust
parts.voice: forensic — close reading of specific phrases, treating the trap as the whole point
body: Certainty of intention doesn't require the word 'trust'. It doesn't require any particular form of words at all — what matters is whether the language, read as a whole and in context, shows the settlor genuinely meant to bind the recipient to a legal obligation, as opposed to expressing a hope, a wish, or moral confidence that the recipient will 'do the right thing'.

That last category has a name: precatory words. Phrases like 'I wish', 'I hope', 'in full confidence that', or 'trusting that she will' were, historically, sometimes read by courts as imposing binding obligations — but the modern approach, reinforced through the nineteenth century, treats precatory language as creating, at most, a moral expectation. A gift given 'in full confidence' that the recipient will use it a certain way is usually just that: a gift, with the recipient free to do as they like, however strongly the donor hoped otherwise.

This is the trap examiners set constantly, because precatory wording often sits inside an otherwise carefully drafted document, surrounded by language that looks formal and legalistic. Read past the surface formality to the actual verb doing the work: does the document say the recipient 'shall hold' the property for someone, or does it say the giver merely 'wishes' or is 'confident' that they will look after someone? The first is imperative and points toward a trust; the second is precatory and, without more, points away from one.

components.definition: Language expressing a hope, wish, or moral confidence (e.g. 'I wish', 'in full confidence that') rather than a binding legal obligation. On its own, precatory language is insufficient to satisfy certainty of intention — it creates a moral expectation, not a trust.

interaction.prompt: A will states: 'I give my house to my son Daniel absolutely, in full confidence that he will allow his sister to live there for as long as she wishes.' Tap the phrase that most strongly signals this is precatory language, not an imperative trust obligation.
interaction.scenarioText: I give my house to my son Daniel absolutely, in full confidence that he will allow his sister to live there for as long as she wishes.
tappableSpans: I give my house to my son Daniel absolutely
allow his sister to live there
for as long as she wishes
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. 'In full confidence that' is a textbook precatory formula — it expresses the testator's hope, not a binding direction, and 'absolutely' earlier in the sentence reinforces that Daniel takes the house as an outright gift.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the phrase that expresses the testator's hope rather than commanding an outcome. 'In full confidence that' is the classic marker of precatory, non-binding language — it sits right next to the gift without controlling it.

parts.heading: Proof without paperwork: trusts inferred from conduct
parts.voice: forensic — examines what courts actually looked at, fact by fact, to infer intention
body: Certainty of intention cuts both ways. Just as formal-sounding language can fail to create a trust, informal, repeated, everyday language and conduct can succeed in creating one — provided it genuinely shows the settlor meant to impose a binding obligation, even without ever using the word 'trust'.

In Paul v Constance, a man separated from his wife and began a relationship with Mrs Paul, without divorcing. He received a personal injury payout and, rather than opening a joint account (which the couple were told they couldn't do, not being married), opened an account in his sole name. He repeatedly told Mrs Paul, in ordinary conversation, 'this money is as much yours as mine', and the couple drew on the account together for shared expenses and even a joint bingo win. The Court of Appeal held this repeated course of conduct and statement was sufficient to show a present intention to hold the account on trust for both of them jointly — despite no formal declaration, no document, and no use of the word 'trust' at any point.

Re Kayford shows the same principle operating in a commercial context. A mail-order company, worried about its own solvency, took legal advice and opened a separate bank account — called the 'Customers' Trust Deposit Account' — into which customer prepayments were paid, kept apart from the company's general funds. Megarry J held a trust was created in favour of the customers, protecting their money from the company's general creditors on insolvency, even though the company itself never formally declared a trust in so many words. What mattered was the substance: money deliberately segregated, with the clear purpose of holding it separately for the customers' benefit, rather than mixing it into the company's own assets.

components.factsShort: A man repeatedly told his partner 'this money is as much yours as mine' about an account in his sole name, and the couple drew on it together.
components.ratioShort: A course of informal conduct and repeated statements can show certainty of intention to create a trust, without any formal declaration or use of the word 'trust'.

expanded.facts: Mr Constance separated from his wife but never divorced, and began living with Mrs Paul. He received compensation for a workplace injury and opened a bank account in his sole name, having been told a joint account with Mrs Paul was not straightforward given his marital status. He repeatedly said the money was 'as much hers as his', and the couple made joint withdrawals, including once splitting a bingo win paid into the same account.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that, on the facts as a whole — the repeated statements and the couple's conduct in dealing with the account jointly — Mr Constance had shown a present intention to declare himself trustee of the account for the benefit of both himself and Mrs Paul, entitling her to a half share on his death.
expanded.significance: This is the leading authority that certainty of intention does not require technical language or a formal document. Ordinary words, said repeatedly and acted on consistently, can be enough — provided, unlike merely precatory language, they show a present, genuine intention to be bound.

interaction.prompt: In Re Kayford, why did the court find a trust had been created over the customer prepayments, even though the company never used the word 'trust' when opening the account?
options: Because any separate bank account automatically creates a trust over its contents
Because the company deliberately segregated the customers' money from its own funds with the clear purpose of holding it apart for their benefit, which showed the necessary intention
Because the customers had signed a written trust deed with the company
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer treats segregation as automatically decisive on its own, regardless of purpose. What actually mattered was that the segregation was done deliberately, for the purpose of protecting the customers' money — the label 'trust' was never used, but the substance of the arrangement supplied the necessary intention.

parts.heading: Certainty of subject matter: what exactly is held on trust?
parts.voice: forensic — close comparison of near-identical wording that lands on opposite sides
body: Certainty of subject matter has two separate limbs, and problem questions routinely test both. First, the trust property itself must be identifiable — you must be able to point to exactly what is held on trust. Second, where there is more than one beneficiary, the beneficial shares must also be certain — you must be able to say how much each beneficiary is entitled to.

Palmer v Simmonds is the classic failure on the first limb. A testator left 'the bulk of my residuary estate' to one beneficiary. 'Bulk' has no fixed legal meaning — is it 60%? 90%? The court held this was too vague to identify the trust property with the certainty a trust requires, and the gift failed on that ground. Contrast that with a gift of 'the sum of £1,000 out of my bank account', or 'my house at 14 Elm Street' — both point to something precise and identifiable, even though only one asset is named out of a larger estate.

The same first-limb problem recurs with unascertained tangible goods. In Re Goldcorp Exchange, customers had paid for gold bullion that was never actually set aside, allocated, or separated from the company's general stock before it went insolvent. The Privy Council held that no trust arose in the customers' favour over any of the bullion, because there was no way to say which specific gold, out of the company's general stock, was supposedly held for which customer. Good intentions to create a trust cannot cure the absence of identifiable property — without segregation, tangible, unascertained goods simply cannot be the subject matter of a trust.

components.factsShort: Customers paid a bullion dealer for gold that was never physically segregated from the company's general stock before insolvency.
components.ratioShort: No trust can arise over unascertained tangible goods that have not been segregated from a larger bulk — there is no identifiable property capable of being held on trust.

expanded.facts: Goldcorp Exchange sold gold bullion to investors, promising to hold specific bullion for each of them, but in practice never physically allocated or set aside any particular bars or stock to particular customers. When the company became insolvent, the customers claimed a proprietary interest in the company's remaining bullion stock, ahead of its general creditors.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Privy Council held that, because the gold each customer supposedly owned had never been identified or separated from the company's general stock, there was no certainty of subject matter and therefore no trust. The customers ranked only as unsecured creditors.
expanded.significance: Goldcorp is the leading modern authority that tangible, unascertained property cannot be the subject matter of a trust without segregation — a rule this lesson's final part will show sits in real tension with how the courts have treated intangible property.

interaction.prompt: Which of these wills is most likely to satisfy certainty of subject matter?
interaction.scenarioA: 'I leave the bulk of my estate to my niece, trusting she will look after the rest of the family.'
interaction.scenarioB: 'I leave the sum of £25,000 from my Barclays current account to my niece, on trust for her and her brother in equal shares.'
interaction.explanation: B identifies a precise sum from a specific account, and states the beneficial shares clearly — both limbs of certainty of subject matter are satisfied. A fails on the first limb exactly as in Palmer v Simmonds: 'the bulk of my estate' has no fixed, identifiable meaning.

parts.heading: The Hunter v Moss problem: shares, gold, and an unresolved tension
parts.voice: forensic and honest — lays out a genuine doctrinal disagreement rather than resolving it artificially
body: Here is where this topic stops being tidy, and you should know that going in rather than being blindsided by it in an exam. In Hunter v Moss, Moss declared himself trustee of 50 out of his holding of 950 identical, unissued shares in a company, without ever identifying which 50 shares out of the 950 were meant. On Goldcorp's logic, that should fail for exactly the same reason bullion failed: no segregation, no identifiable subject matter, no trust.

The Court of Appeal upheld the trust anyway. Its reasoning was that, because the shares were all identical and fungible — unlike bars of gold, which can vary slightly and be physically distinguished — it made no practical difference which 50 of the 950 were held on trust, so segregation wasn't necessary to know what the beneficiary was entitled to.

Be honest with yourself, and with an examiner, about what this actually is: a genuinely contested exception, not a neat rule that sits comfortably alongside Goldcorp. Critics have pointed out that Goldcorp itself involved fungible gold bullion too, and that the tangible/intangible distinction Hunter v Moss relies on has never been fully or convincingly explained — shares are intangible property, gold is tangible, but the practical problem (which units belong to whom) looks identical either way. The safest position for you to take in an answer is not to pretend the tension doesn't exist: state that Hunter v Moss is generally treated as good law for intangible, fungible property such as shares, while Re Goldcorp Exchange governs tangible, unascertained goods, and flag that the doctrinal justification for treating the two differently remains genuinely debated among academics and judges.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that Hunter v Moss and Re Goldcorp Exchange are simply inconsistent authorities, with one obviously wrong, or alternatively pretend there is no tension between them at all.
components.whyItsWrong: Neither extreme is defensible in an exam. The accepted (if contested) reconciliation is that Hunter v Moss is confined to intangible, fungible property like shares, where segregation is said to make no practical difference to what is held on trust, while Re Goldcorp Exchange governs tangible, unascertained goods like bullion, where it does. The stronger answer acknowledges the doctrinal tension honestly rather than asserting a false consistency or a false contradiction.

interaction.prompt: Aisha owns 300 identical, fully paid ordinary shares in a private company. She tells her brother, in writing, 'I hold 100 of my 300 shares in this company on trust for you', without identifying which 100 shares. Analyse whether a valid trust is created over the 100 shares.
factsToOrder: She declares herself trustee of 100 of them for her brother
The 100 shares are never identified or segregated from the other 200
The shares are intangible, fungible property, unlike physical bullion

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a trust of 100 unidentified shares out of a larger identical holding satisfies certainty of subject matter.
modelAnswer.rule: Certainty of subject matter normally requires the trust property to be identified or segregated (Palmer v Simmonds; Re Goldcorp Exchange for tangible, unascertained goods). Hunter v Moss holds that, for intangible, fungible property such as shares, a trust of an unsegregated part of a larger identical holding can still satisfy certainty of subject matter, because it makes no practical difference which units are held on trust — though this remains a doctrinally contested exception.
modelAnswer.application: Aisha's 300 shares are identical and fungible, like the shares in Hunter v Moss, and unlike the bullion in Re Goldcorp Exchange. Applying Hunter v Moss, the absence of segregation should not be fatal here, because it makes no practical difference which 100 of the 300 shares are the trust property — the brother's entitlement is to 100 shares of that class, however they are ultimately identified. A rigorous answer should note the doctrinal criticism of this approach and its uncertain reconciliation with Goldcorp.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Following Hunter v Moss, a valid trust of 100 shares is most likely created despite the lack of segregation, though the point is not free from academic and judicial controversy.

testPool.prompt: Which case established the three certainties required for a valid express trust?
testPool.modelAnswer: Knight v Knight (1840) 3 Beav 148, per Lord Langdale MR: certainty of intention, subject matter, and objects.

testPool.prompt: What happens to a purported trust if certainty of subject matter is missing?
options: The trust fails entirely
The trust is valid but the trustee gets to choose the property
The court fills the gap by ordering an equal division of the whole estate

testPool.prompt: Which of these best describes precatory words?
options: Language expressing a hope or moral confidence, insufficient on its own to show certainty of intention
Any language used in a will, regardless of its content
Language that automatically creates a binding trust because it appears in a formal legal document
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming formality of the document guarantees a binding trust. Precatory words remain precatory — expressing hope, not obligation — wherever they appear, however formal the surrounding document looks.

testPool.prompt: In Palmer v Simmonds, why did the gift of 'the bulk of my residuary estate' fail?
options: Because 'bulk' has no fixed, identifiable meaning, so the trust property was uncertain
Because residuary estates can never be held on trust
Because the beneficiary had died before the testator

testPool.prompt: Tap the phrase in this clause that is precatory rather than imperative.
testPool.scenarioText: I give the sum of £50,000 to my husband, hoping that he will use some of it to support our daughter through university.
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. 'Hoping that' signals a wish, not a command — the husband takes the £50,000 as an outright gift, free of any binding trust obligation to his daughter.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Find the word that expresses the testator's wish rather than a binding direction. 'Hoping that' is the classic precatory signal here, not the identification of the sum or the recipient.

testPool.prompt: A father repeatedly tells his adult daughter, over several years and in front of witnesses, 'this house is as much yours as mine', and they jointly pay the mortgage and bills, though the house remains registered in his sole name. Applying Paul v Constance, is certainty of intention likely satisfied?
options: Yes — the repeated statements and consistent joint conduct can show a present intention to hold the property on trust for both of them
No — without a signed trust deed, informal statements can never satisfy certainty of intention
No — registration in his sole name is conclusive and cannot be displaced by anything he says
testPool.explanation: Paul v Constance confirms that a course of repeated statements and consistent conduct, taken together, can show the necessary intention without any formal document — legal title in one name is the starting point, not the end of the analysis.

testPool.prompt: A struggling travel agency, on legal advice, opens a bank account separate from its trading account and pays all customer deposits into it as soon as they're received, intending to protect customers if the business fails. It never uses the word 'trust'. Applying Re Kayford, is a trust likely created over the deposits?
options: Yes — deliberate segregation for the purpose of protecting the customers' money can show the necessary intention, even without the word 'trust'
No — without the word 'trust' being used, intention can never be shown
No — only individually named accounts per customer can create a trust
testPool.explanation: Re Kayford confirms that the substance of deliberately segregating funds for a protective purpose can supply certainty of intention, regardless of the label used — exactly as with the 'Customers' Trust Deposit Account' in that case.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario most closely mirrors the reasoning that failed in Re Goldcorp Exchange?
testPool.scenarioA: A wine merchant sells 50 cases of a specific vintage to a customer and physically sets those 50 cases aside in a marked section of the warehouse.
testPool.scenarioB: A wine merchant sells 50 cases of a specific vintage to a customer, takes payment, but keeps all stock of that vintage mixed together in the general warehouse with no cases set aside for that customer.
testPool.explanation: B mirrors Goldcorp exactly: unascertained, unsegregated goods mixed into a general stock, with no way to say which units belong to which buyer — certainty of subject matter fails. A, with physical segregation, would likely succeed.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below describing Re Goldcorp Exchange, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: Customers had paid for bullion that the company promised to hold on their behalf. In practice, no bullion was ever physically set aside or allocated to any individual customer before the company's insolvency. Because the property said to be held on trust was never identified or separated from the company's general stock, there was no certainty of subject matter and no trust arose. The customers ranked only as unsecured creditors.
testPool.ratioSentence: Because the property said to be held on trust was never identified or separated from the company's general stock, there was no certainty of subject matter and no trust arose.

testPool.prompt: What is the best statement of how Hunter v Moss and Re Goldcorp Exchange currently fit together?
options: They cannot be reconciled at all, and one of them must simply be wrong

Hunter v Moss is generally treated as confined to intangible, fungible property like shares, while Goldcorp governs tangible, unascertained goods — though the justification for the distinction remains genuinely debated
They are perfectly consistent, because shares and bullion are treated identically by the courts
testPool.trapExplanation: Both extremes overstate the position. The accepted, examinable position is the narrower one: courts and academics generally distinguish the two by tangibility, while acknowledging — rather than hiding — that the distinction's doctrinal justification is contested.

testPool.prompt: A will leaves '£10,000 to be divided between my two sons' without stating the proportions each should receive. Which limb of certainty of subject matter is at risk here?
options: Certainty of the beneficial shares
Certainty of the trust property itself
Certainty of objects

testPool.prompt: A father tells his son, in a signed letter, 'I want you to have my car when I'm gone, and I trust you'll let your sister use it whenever she needs to.' Analyse whether the son takes the car subject to a binding trust obligation in his sister's favour.
factsToOrder: The letter gives the car to the son
The letter adds 'I trust you'll let your sister use it whenever she needs to'

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether 'I trust you'll let your sister use it whenever she needs to' imposes a binding trust obligation on the son, or is merely precatory.
modelAnswer.rule: Certainty of intention requires language showing a genuine intention to impose a binding obligation, not merely a hope or moral expectation (Knight v Knight). Precatory words such as 'I trust that' or 'I hope' are, without more, insufficient on their own (contrast the informal but repeated, present-tense assurances found sufficient in Paul v Constance).
modelAnswer.application: 'I trust you'll let your sister use it whenever she needs to' is precatory in form — it expresses a hope about future conduct rather than a present, binding direction, and stands in contrast to the clear, repeated, present-tense assurances in Paul v Constance. There is no course of conduct here reinforcing an intention to bind, only a single letter with soft, hopeful language.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The son most likely takes the car as an outright gift, free of any binding trust in his sister's favour; the wording is precatory, not imperative.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a student should work through when checking certainty of subject matter on a problem question.
items: Identify exactly what property is said to be held on trust
Check whether that property is identified or segregated from any larger bulk
If there is more than one beneficiary, check whether their beneficial shares are also certain
Conclude whether the trust survives on subject matter, or fails and the property results back

testPool.prompt: In Hunter v Moss, what type of property was the subject of the disputed trust?
options: Shares — intangible, fungible property
Gold bullion — tangible property
Land

testPool.prompt: A collector owns 40 identical, mass-produced commemorative coins with no individually distinguishing marks, and declares himself trustee of 10 of them for his nephew without identifying which 10. Which authority gives the strongest argument that this trust can still succeed despite the lack of segregation?
options: Hunter v Moss, by analogy — the coins are fungible and identical, so it arguably makes no practical difference which 10 are held on trust
Re Goldcorp Exchange, because the coins are tangible property
Palmer v Simmonds, because the coins form part of a larger collection
testPool.explanation: This is a genuinely debatable extension: the coins, though tangible like the bullion in Goldcorp, are also identical and fungible like the shares in Hunter v Moss. The strongest supporting authority for validity is Hunter v Moss's fungibility reasoning, though a well-reasoned answer would flag that the coins' tangibility (unlike shares) makes the analogy to Goldcorp's tangible-goods rule arguable the other way too.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The two mistakes that recur most in this lesson's test items are: treating precatory words as binding just because they sit in a formal document, and treating Hunter v Moss as a clean, uncontroversial rule rather than a contested exception to the segregation requirement that governs tangible property in Re Goldcorp Exchange.
